# Edge and On-Device Deployment {#sec-edge}

An on-device model is one component of an application that must work across
different processors, operating-system versions, memory conditions, battery
states, and network conditions. The unit that is tested and released is
therefore a **versioned device deployment**: the model, tokenizer, prompt
template, compiled graph, quantization scheme, runtime, routing policy, and
supported device class that together produced a result.

Local execution is useful when a feature needs an offline path, a short and
predictable response loop, or a narrower data boundary, meaning that user data
reaches fewer systems. It is justified only when the complete feature also
meets its quality, memory, energy, thermal, and support requirements. The model decision from @sec-choosing-model and the
serving contract from @sec-serving-stack still apply; the difference is that
qualification happens on a heterogeneous fleet rather than a controlled server
pool. Along the way, the chapter names the current on-device models, runtimes,
and platform services and what each is built for.

## Freeze the device support envelope

A **device support envelope** states where the feature is supported and what
“supported” means. It is derived from the feature; the parameter count and the
runtime are chosen afterward to fit it. The envelope turns “run this model
locally” into a claim that can be tested and withdrawn.

| Concern | What the envelope fixes |
|---|---|
| Task and quality | Task class, input and output limits, languages, safety policy, quality threshold, and rejection behavior |
| Data boundary | Data classes allowed locally, data classes eligible for upload, retention, and whether cloud use requires explicit consent |
| Device population | Representative device tier, processor or accelerator requirements, minimum OS and runtime versions, and available storage |
| User experience | Cold-start and warm-start latency, time to first token, time per output token, cancellation, partial output, and accessibility behavior |
| Resource limits | Peak resident memory, sustained energy, thermal state, background-load assumptions, and concurrency |
| Availability | Model installation state, offline behavior, fallback policy, and behavior when neither route is available |
| Lifecycle | Artifact owner, rollout cohort, telemetry boundary, rollback target, retirement date, and requalification triggers |

The support envelope is narrower than “all recent phones.” A useful device tier
names the properties that affect execution: OS build, runtime version, system-on-chip
family, memory class, storage headroom, and available backend. Marketing names
alone are insufficient because devices sold under one family can have different
memory or thermal behavior.

Represent the envelope as an **acceptance matrix**. Rows are supported device
tiers; columns are relevant states such as cold and warm process, model absent
and installed, normal and low storage, normal and low battery, foreground and
background load, offline and weak network, and cool and thermally constrained.
Each cell records pass, fail, or unsupported against the same envelope. The
matrix shows gaps before a rollout instead of through user reports after it.

## Count what must fit

Raw parameter size is only the first term in the memory budget. For a decoder
model, which generates its output one token at a time, a useful planning
approximation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_{\mathrm{weights}}
  &\gtrsim \frac{N_{\mathrm{params}} b_w}{8} + M_{\mathrm{metadata}}, \\
M_{\mathrm{KV}}
  &= \frac{2 B L n_{\mathrm{kv}} d_h S b_{\mathrm{kv}}}{8}, \\
M_{\mathrm{peak}}
  &= M_{\mathrm{weights}} + M_{\mathrm{KV}}
   + M_{\mathrm{workspace}} + M_{\mathrm{runtime}} + M_{\mathrm{app}}, \\
M_{\mathrm{peak}}
  &\le M_{\mathrm{budget}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $M_{\mathrm{weights}}$ is the stored weight footprint;
$N_{\mathrm{params}}$ is the number of parameters; $b_w$ is the average stored
bits per parameter after quantization, the conversion of weights to a
lower-precision number format; the constant $8$ converts bits to bytes; and
$M_{\mathrm{metadata}}$ covers quantization scales, zero points, block headers,
tensor alignment, and other format data. The first line is an inequality
because the packed-tensor calculation gives a lower bound on both installed
size and resident memory.

$M_{\mathrm{KV}}$ is the uncompressed planning size of the key-value cache,
the attention state that decoding keeps for every processed token so that
earlier tokens are not recomputed; the factor $2$ accounts for keys and values;
$B$ is the number of concurrent sequences; $L$ is the number of transformer
layers; $n_{\mathrm{kv}}$ is the
number of key-value heads per layer; $d_h$ is the head dimension; $S$ is the
number of cached tokens per sequence; and $b_{\mathrm{kv}}$ is the stored bits
per cache element. Runtime-specific padding, cache layout, sliding windows, or
cross-layer sharing can change the measured value.

$M_{\mathrm{workspace}}$ covers activations (the intermediate values each
layer produces), temporary buffers, compiled kernels, and backend workspaces.
$M_{\mathrm{runtime}}$ is the inference runtime and its loaded libraries. $M_{\mathrm{app}}$ is everything else the application
needs while inference runs. Their sum is peak resident memory
$M_{\mathrm{peak}}$, which must remain below the memory available to the feature,
$M_{\mathrm{budget}}$. The budget is smaller than the device's advertised RAM,
because the OS, other processes, graphics, media, and the application itself
already use part of that memory.

A 3-billion-parameter model at four bits has a raw packed-weight payload of
1.5 GB. That arithmetic is a necessary check: it rejects impossible candidates,
and a candidate that passes it still has to be measured. Quantization metadata,
tensor alignment, context-dependent cache growth, runtime allocations, and
memory pressure can move the actual peak materially. Measure the exported
artifact in the real process, including its longest supported context and its
worst supported input.

Which count enters $N_{\mathrm{params}}$ is itself a property of the artifact.
Gemma 4's edge models are published with two counts: E2B has 2.3 billion
effective parameters and 5.1 billion including its per-layer embeddings, and
E4B has 4.5 and 8 billion [@google2026gemma4]. The per-layer embedding tables
are used only for lookups, so they add storage without adding matrix
multiplication. The installed size follows the total; whether the tables also
occupy accelerator memory depends on where the runtime keeps them, which is one
more reason $M_{\mathrm{peak}}$ is measured rather than derived.

An on-device model reaches an application in one of two ways, and the choice
changes who owns the fingerprint. A **platform model** ships with the operating
system: the application calls a system API and downloads nothing, but the
platform decides when the model changes, so the model version the platform
reports belongs in the deployment fingerprint and an OS update is a
requalification trigger. An **app-shipped model** is an open-weight artifact
that the application downloads and runs in a runtime it bundles. The
application then controls the version and carries its storage, delivery, and
qualification on every supported device tier, as the delivery section below
describes.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Apple's on-device foundation model has about 3 billion parameters. Its decoder
weights are stored at 2 bits after quantization-aware training, its embedding
table at 4 bits, and its KV cache at 8 bits. Its layers are split into two
blocks in a 5:3 ratio, and the second block reuses the KV cache of the first,
which cuts cache memory by 37.5 percent [@apple2025fmupdates]. Applications reach it, and the larger model in Private
Cloud Compute, through the Foundation Models framework on iOS, iPadOS, macOS,
and visionOS 26 and later [@apple2026foundationmodels]. On Android, Google's
April 2026 AICore developer preview serves Gemma 4 E2B and E4B through the ML
Kit Prompt API as the base of the next Gemini Nano generation
[@android2026aicore]. Among app-shipped models, Gemma 4 E2B and E4B are
released under Apache 2.0 and accept text, image, and audio input with a
128K-token context [@google2026gemma4]. Microsoft's BitNet b1.58 2B4T has 2.4
billion parameters trained as ternary weights on 4 trillion tokens and runs
through the MIT-licensed bitnet.cpp [@microsoft2026bitnetrepo].
:::

KIVI gives one reason to budget the cache separately from the weights. Its
authors found different distributions in keys and values and evaluated
per-channel key and per-token value quantization rather than treating the cache
as ordinary model weights [@liu2024kivi]. The finding holds for the models and
runtime they evaluated. It justifies testing cache quantization on the target
artifact, and it does not show that a two-bit cache is lossless for other
models or tasks.

## Measure the path and the device state

The local and remote paths have different latency components. For an installed
local artifact,

$$
T_{\mathrm{local}}
= T_{\mathrm{load}} + T_{\mathrm{prefill}}
+ \sum_{k=1}^{O} T_{\mathrm{decode},k} + T_{\mathrm{post}},
$$

where $T_{\mathrm{load}}$ is model load and specialization time;
$T_{\mathrm{prefill}}$ processes the input; $O$ is the number of output tokens;
$T_{\mathrm{decode},k}$ is the time for output token $k$; and
$T_{\mathrm{post}}$ covers validation, rendering, and any feature-specific
post-processing. A remote path instead includes upload, network, provider queue,
remote execution, and download time. Which path is faster depends on state: a
cold local load can take longer than a call to a warm remote service, while a
warm local model avoids variable network delay.

For batch-one autoregressive decode, where a single sequence produces one token
per step, a bandwidth estimate gives an upper bound:

$$
R_{\mathrm{decode}} \lesssim \frac{BW_{\mathrm{eff}}}{D_{\mathrm{token}}}.
$$

Here $R_{\mathrm{decode}}$ is generated tokens per second;
$BW_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is effective memory bandwidth in bytes per second under the
measured device state; and $D_{\mathrm{token}}$ is bytes moved from memory per
generated token. This is a bandwidth ceiling, not a prediction. Prefill can be
compute-bound, some weights or cache blocks may be reused, and unpacking,
dequantization, unsupported operators, synchronization, or small kernels can
become the bottleneck. Roofline analysis, which bounds a workload's throughput
by the device's peak arithmetic rate and its memory bandwidth, turns these
effects into a hypothesis about a specific workload [@yuan2024llmroofline].
Whether lower precision increases speed on a given device is then settled by
measurement.

```{figure}
//| figure: device-memory-budget
//| label: fig-edge-memory-budget
//| fig-cap: "Peak resident memory $M_{\mathrm{peak}}$ against cached tokens $S$ (top) and the batch-one decode ceiling $BW_{\mathrm{eff}}/D_{\mathrm{token}}$ (bottom), from the memory and bandwidth equations above, with every weight byte and the whole cache read once per generated token. Defaults are illustrative planning values: 3 billion parameters at 4 bits, $L = 28$, $n_{\mathrm{kv}} = 8$, $d_h = 128$, $S = 4{,}096$, an 8-bit cache, and 1.1 GB for the runtime, application, and workspaces, with one 16-bit scale per 32 weights drawn as $M_{\mathrm{metadata}}$; the memory budget and effective bandwidth are illustrative stand-ins for a device tier's measured values. Hatching marks contexts that exceed the budget. A lower-bit cache moves the fit point to longer contexts and slows the fall of the ceiling; the weight format shifts both curves at every length."
```

Measure at least cold start, warm start, time to first token, time per output
token, end-to-end latency, peak resident memory, error rate, and quality on the
same task set. Report p50 and p95 rather than one best run. Also measure energy
per accepted task, not energy per token alone. A useful device-side estimate is

$$
E_{\mathrm{task}} = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \left(P(t)-P_{\mathrm{idle}}\right)\,dt,
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{task}}$ is incremental task energy; $t_0$ and $t_1$ bound the
complete feature interaction; $P(t)$ is measured device power at time $t$; and
$P_{\mathrm{idle}}$ is the comparable idle baseline. If the platform exposes
only energy proxies, label them as proxies and keep the measurement method
stable across candidates.

Short bursts hide thermal throttling, the main way a device's performance
degrades under sustained load. A sustained run continues until latency, power,
and temperature reach thermal steady state or the test limit. Record battery
state, charging state, ambient condition, power mode, screen state, background
load, and frequency throttling. Both Android and Apple expose
thermal-state signals that applications can observe; those signals should be
part of a controlled test and, where appropriate, a runtime admission decision
[@androidThermal; @appleThermal]. MLPerf Mobile likewise treats the model,
software stack, device, accuracy target, and run rules as one benchmarked system
[@reddi2022mlperfmobile].

## Compression is a system choice

Compression is valuable only when the resulting artifact retains task quality
and the target backend executes its representation efficiently. The weight
format, activation format, and KV-cache format are recorded as three separate
decisions, because they affect different memory regions and require different
kernel support. @sec-quantization-kernels develops the underlying
representations and kernels; the concern here is qualifying their exported
device artifact.

| Mechanism | What changes | What it can buy | What must be checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small-by-design architecture | Depth, width, attention layout, embeddings, or weight sharing | A better quality/latency point within a small parameter budget | Task transfer, supported operators, cache size, and measured latency |
| Distillation | A student learns from teacher outputs or distributions | More capability in a smaller student for the trained task distribution | Teacher errors, coverage gaps, safety behavior, and independent evaluation |
| Structured pruning | Heads, channels, layers, or blocks are removed | A smaller graph that may map to existing kernels | Retraining cost, quality loss, and whether the backend accelerates the new shape |
| Post-training quantization | A trained checkpoint is calibrated and encoded at lower precision | Lower storage and often lower weight traffic without full retraining | Calibration set coverage, task-specific evaluation, kernel availability, and dequantization cost |
| Quantization-aware training | Quantization effects are simulated during training or adaptation | Better recovery at aggressive precision | Training cost, exact deployment format, and export parity |
| Low-bit pretraining | The model is trained for a low-bit or discrete representation from the start | A representation designed around the target arithmetic | Lack of a simple conversion path, immature kernels, and evidence at the intended scale |
| KV-cache quantization | Attention keys and values use fewer bits | Longer context or lower peak memory | Cache layout, accuracy across context lengths, and attention-kernel support |

MobileLLM is evidence for designing within a small budget. Its authors studied
deep-and-thin sub-billion models, embedding sharing, grouped-query attention (in
which groups of query heads share one key and value head), and
adjacent-block sharing instead of compressing a much larger checkpoint
[@liu2024mobilellm]. Its 350-million-parameter model came close to LLaMA 2 7B
on API-calling tasks, a model twenty times smaller on a task suited to it.
OpenELM varies width by layer instead of using one width throughout and reports
2.36 percent higher accuracy than OLMo at about one billion parameters with half
the pretraining tokens [@mehta2024openelm]. These results motivate architecture
search in the intended size range; the best shape can still differ across tasks
and devices.

Distillation and training length supply much of the rest of a small model's
quality. Gemma 2 trains its 2B and 9B models on a larger teacher's full
next-token distribution instead of one-hot labels [@gemma2024]. Small models are
also trained far past the compute-optimal point. About 20 tokens per parameter
minimizes training compute, but a deployed model pays inference cost on every
request, so over a long service life a smaller model trained on more tokens
costs less in total [@sardana2024beyond]. Gemma 2 gave its 2B model 2 trillion
tokens and its 9B model 8 trillion, roughly 40 times the compute-optimal count
[@gemma2024], and MiniCPM measured its own optimal ratio at about 192 tokens per
parameter [@hu2024minicpm]. The pruning row takes the opposite route. Sheared
LLaMA prunes LLaMA 2 7B to 1.3-billion and 2.7-billion-parameter shapes and
continues pretraining on a small fraction of the original tokens
[@xia2023sheared]. That is efficient to produce, but the result inherits an
architecture chosen for a server.

For post-training quantization, the **calibration set**, the sample of inputs
used to set the quantization ranges, is part of the artifact. It should cover
real prompt lengths, languages, modalities, tool schemas, and rare but important
request classes. AWQ uses observed activations to protect salient weight
channels in a weight-only method [@lin2024awq]. SmoothQuant moves some
quantization difficulty from activations into weights to support W8A8 execution,
with 8-bit weights and 8-bit activations [@xiao2023smoothquant]. These methods
solve different problems, so a paper's aggregate benchmark does not substitute
for task-specific evaluation on the exact artifact and exact backend.

Underneath both lies one obstacle: a few values far larger than the rest. In
activations, a few dimensions carry such magnitudes, and LLM.int8() keeps
those dimensions in higher precision [@dettmers2022llmint8]. Weights are better
behaved, which is why edge formats quantize weights hardest, with weight-only
methods such as GPTQ's second-order error correction [@frantar2022gptq] and AWQ.
Formats also limit the reach of any outlier by giving each small block of
weights its own scale. The runnable below quantizes one weight matrix that
contains 16 large weights, with one 16-bit scale for the whole tensor, per 256
weights, and per 32 weights. It reports the stored bits per weight $b_w$, the
share of weights stored as zero, and the relative error of the layer's output.
A single scale spends the 4-bit range on the outliers and rounds most ordinary
weights to zero; a scale per 32 weights costs half a bit more per weight and
brings the error close to that of the same matrix without outliers, which is
the $M_{\mathrm{metadata}}$ term of the memory budget at work. Setting
`BITS = 2` shows why 2-bit production models are trained for their format
rather than rounded after training: even 32-weight blocks leave a large error.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np

BITS = 4                                        # stored bits per weight
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
W = rng.normal(0, 0.02, (256, 1024))            # one layer's weight matrix
W.flat[rng.choice(W.size, 16, replace=False)] = 0.4   # 16 outlier weights
x = rng.normal(0, 1, 1024)

def quantize(W, block):
    """Round to nearest with one float16 scale per block of weights."""
    B = W.reshape(-1, block)
    qmax = 2 ** (BITS - 1) - 1
    scale = (np.abs(B).max(axis=1, keepdims=True) / qmax).astype(np.float16).astype(float)
    q = np.clip(np.round(B / scale), -qmax - 1, qmax)       # the stored integers
    return (q * scale).reshape(W.shape), BITS + 16 / block  # weights, b_w

errors = []
for block in [W.size, 256, 32]:
    Wq, b_w = quantize(W, block)
    errors.append(np.linalg.norm((Wq - W) @ x) / np.linalg.norm(W @ x))
    print(f"one scale per {block:>6} weights: b_w = {b_w:.3f}, "
          f"{np.mean(Wq == 0):3.0%} stored as zero, output error {errors[-1]:.1%}")
assert errors[0] > errors[1] > errors[2]        # smaller blocks, smaller error
```
::::

Quantization-aware training and low-bit pretraining become relevant when
post-training quality is insufficient. Below four bits, rounding error stops
being a small perturbation that trained weights absorb. Quantization-aware
training simulates the rounding in the forward pass and passes gradients through
it as if it were the identity, the straight-through estimator, so the network
learns weights that survive the format. One published Apple model used two-bit
quantization-aware training with learnable weight clipping, together with
KV-cache sharing, for an approximately 3-billion-parameter on-device model, and
then trained low-rank adapters to recover the quality lost to compression
[@li2025applemodels; @apple2025fmupdates]. BitNet first trained binary weights
from scratch [@wang2023bitnet], and BitNet b1.58 reports ternary weights in
$\{-1,0,1\}$ for models trained in that representation [@ma2024bitnet]. In the mathematical dot product, a ternary weight replaces a
general weight multiplication with selection, sign change, or zero. A deployed
system still has scales, activation processing, attention, normalization,
packing, and memory traffic. Zero-valued weights are not automatically
structured sparsity, a regular pattern of zeros that hardware can skip, and a
backend saves work only if its kernel exploits the representation. Follow-up
work quantizes the activations of these models to 4 bits [@wang2024bitneta48]
and supplies CPU kernels written for the ternary format [@wang2024bitnetcpp],
which is the backend support such a gain depends on.

## Build a deployable artifact

A source checkpoint has to be converted before a device can run it. Export and
lowering specialize a graph to an operator set, memory plan, tensor layout,
precision, and backend. ExecuTorch, for example, separates export and
ahead-of-time lowering from its device runtime and produces programs for
selected backends [@executorchDocs].
Core ML can schedule supported work across CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine, but the
actual compute plan and compatibility still depend on the converted model and
target OS [@appleCoreML]. A container such as GGUF can carry tensors and model
metadata, yet a runtime build must still implement the architecture, tokenizer
semantics, quantization types, and required operators [@ggufSpec].
Compatibility is therefore a property of an artifact together with a specific
runtime build.

Record a **deployment fingerprint** with at least:

- source checkpoint and immutable revision;
- tokenizer, special tokens, and prompt template;
- adapter set (small trained weight additions to the base model) and merge
  state;
- export graph and exporter version;
- quantization configuration and calibration-set revision;
- compiled artifact format and cryptographic digest;
- runtime version and linked operator set;
- backend delegate, fallback partitions, and compute policy;
- supported OS build, ABI, and device class; and
- routing, safety, context, and sampling policies.

The fingerprint prevents a common diagnostic failure: comparing “the same
model” when one build changed its template, exporter, quantization, or backend.
It also supplies the key for every quality result and device metric.

Before performance testing, establish semantic parity. Run golden prompts
through the source graph and compiled artifact; compare tokenization, structured
output, stop handling, and task results within declared tolerances. Inspect the
partition plan for unsupported operators; the plan assigns each part of the
graph either to an accelerator backend (a delegate) or to the CPU. A silent CPU
fallback may preserve correctness while making latency or energy unacceptable,
so the capability probe, the on-device check of what the runtime will execute
where, must report the actual backend delegate and every CPU fallback.

### Runtimes and accelerator paths

An app-shipped model runs in a runtime the application bundles, and the runtime
fixes the artifact format, the quantization types, and the backends a device
tier can use. Each is one entry of the fingerprint.

| Runtime | Artifact | License | Backends | Built for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **llama.cpp** | GGUF with block and k-quant formats [@llamacpp; @ikawrakow2023kquants] | MIT | CPUs, Metal, CUDA, HIP, Vulkan, SYCL, OpenCL on Adreno GPUs, Hexagon on Snapdragon | A portable path across laptops, desktops, and phones |
| **MLX and MLX LM** | Checkpoints converted and quantized by MLX LM [@mlx2023; @mlxlm2026repo] | MIT | Apple silicon GPUs through Metal, with arrays in unified memory; CUDA and CPU on Linux | Macs |
| **LiteRT-LM** | `.litertlm` files on LiteRT, the successor to TensorFlow Lite [@google2026litertlm] | Apache 2.0 | CPU, GPU, and NPU on Android, iOS, web, desktop, and IoT devices | Google's on-device stack and cross-platform mobile apps |
| **ExecuTorch** | PyTorch programs exported and lowered ahead of time [@executorch] | BSD | XNNPACK on CPUs; Core ML, Vulkan, and MLX; Qualcomm, MediaTek, Samsung Exynos, Arm, and NXP accelerators; microcontrollers | Teams whose models are written in PyTorch |
| **ONNX Runtime GenAI** | ONNX graphs [@microsoft2026ortgenai] | MIT | CPU, CUDA, DirectML, QNN for Qualcomm NPUs, OpenVINO, WebGPU | Windows PCs and cross-vendor NPUs |
| **MLC LLM** | Models compiled per target by machine-learning compilation [@mlcllm; @chen2018tvm] | Apache 2.0 | CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan, Metal, OpenCL on Adreno and Mali GPUs, WebGPU in the browser | One model compiled for many targets, including browsers |

The dedicated accelerators are faster per watt than the CPU, and they are also
where the device fleet fragments. Apple's Neural Engine is reached through Core
ML and rewards transformer layouts rewritten for it
[@apple2022anetransformers]. Qualcomm's Hexagon NPU is reached through the
Qualcomm AI Engine Direct SDK, to which TensorFlow Lite and ONNX Runtime
delegate work [@qualcomm-qnn]. Mobile GPUs are reached through OpenCL, Vulkan,
or Metal. Each path has its own operator coverage, quantization formats, and
compiler behavior, so one source model does not yield one executable. A
portable CPU build is the floor that runs on every supported tier, and an
accelerator path is added per tier where the partition plan shows the exported
graph actually runs on it.

Three mechanisms recover speed and memory within a runtime. Speculative
decoding lets a small draft model propose several tokens that the deployed
model verifies in one forward pass, which turns part of a memory-bound serial
decode into batched work without changing the output distribution
[@leviathan2023fast]. KV-cache sharing across layers shrinks the cache, the
largest memory consumer after the weights [@li2025applemodels]. Adapter
swapping keeps one frozen base model resident while small low-rank adapters
specialize it per feature [@hu2021lora], so each feature adds a small fraction
of the base model's size rather than a second model. Each mechanism is a runtime capability, and each needs its
own entry in the fingerprint and its own parity check.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

The latest releases include LiteRT-LM v0.16.0, which runs Gemma 4, Gemma 3n,
Llama, Phi-4, and Qwen models and powers on-device features in Chrome and on
Pixel Watch [@google2026litertlm], and ONNX Runtime GenAI v0.11.5, which powers
Foundry Local and Windows ML on Windows [@microsoft2026ortgenai]. llama.cpp
lists 17 backends, including Hexagon for Snapdragon NPUs and OpenCL for Adreno
GPUs [@llamacpp]. ExecuTorch's CUDA and WebGPU backends are experimental
[@executorch]. bitnet.cpp reports CPU speedups for ternary models of 1.37 to
5.07 times on Arm and 2.37 to 6.17 times on x86, measured by its authors, and
lists NPU support as future work [@microsoft2026bitnetrepo].
:::

## Make hybrid routing explicit

Hybrid execution is governed by a routing policy that chooses the path before a
request runs, instead of sending whatever fails locally to the cloud. The route
is a function of four inputs:

$$
r(x,d,s,p) \in \{\mathrm{local},\ \mathrm{cloud},\ \mathrm{decline}\},
$$

where $x$ is the request and its task class; $d$ is its data classification;
$s$ is current device state, including model availability, memory, thermal,
battery, and connectivity; $p$ is the versioned product policy; and $r$ is the
selected route. “Decline” includes asking the user to download the model, wait,
change a setting, or perform the task elsewhere.

```{figure}
//| figure: hybrid-route
//| label: fig-edge-tier
//| fig-cap: "The routing function $r(x,d,s,p)$, evaluated before any model runs. The local route needs every local check, including $T_{\mathrm{local}} = T_{\mathrm{load}} + T_{\mathrm{prefill}} + \sum_k T_{\mathrm{decode},k} + T_{\mathrm{post}}$ within the remaining deadline; the cloud route needs an upload-eligible data class, explicit permission, a network, and $T_{\mathrm{cloud}}$ within the deadline. The policy takes local when it qualifies, cloud when only cloud does, and otherwise declines with the failed check and what to offer the user. Bold marks the first check that rules a route out. Task sizes, rates, and times are illustrative."
```

For a **local-only** request, model unavailable, low storage, or thermal pressure
must lead to a local error or decline path, and the request is never uploaded.
A **cloud-eligible** request needs the declared legal and product basis and any
explicit consent before transmission. If permission is absent, there is no
silent fallback. If both routes are allowed, the router chooses by measured
quality and the remaining deadline rather than by an impression that the
request is “hard.”

The router should route before execution whenever possible, because falling
back after partial output can duplicate text, change semantics, or expose data
the user expected to remain local. If a local run fails after producing a
partial output, it terminates with a typed reason, an error code from a
declared set, and the versioned product policy determines whether the user may
start a new cloud attempt. A cloud continuation is never appended without the
user seeing it. The result carries its execution provenance (local, cloud, or
declined) so the UI, telemetry, and support tools can report which path
produced it.

Platform models ship both routes as system services. Apple's Foundation Models
framework gives an application the on-device model and, when a request needs
more reasoning or context, the larger model in Private Cloud Compute
[@apple2026foundationmodels]. Private Cloud Compute narrows the cloud route's
data boundary by construction: its stated requirements include stateless
computation, no privileged runtime access, and verifiable transparency, under
which the server software is published for researchers to inspect
[@apple2024pcc]. On Android, AICore serves the on-device model to applications
through the ML Kit Prompt API [@android2026aicore]. The platform supplies the
routes and their guarantees; the product policy $p$ still decides which
requests may take the cloud route and whether the user has agreed to it.

## Map the complete data flow

Keeping inference in the app can reduce transmission and server retention, but
it is not, by itself, a privacy guarantee. Input or output may still reach
temporary files, clipboard history, backups, keyboard services, shared caches,
analytics SDKs, crash reports, telemetry, tools, or a cloud fallback. The model
and its personalization data can also reveal sensitive behavior if stored
without the app sandbox and platform protections.

Draw a data-flow map for the complete feature. For each surface, record purpose,
data class, retention, protection, recipient, deletion path, and whether the
surface works offline. Apply the same security review used for other mobile
data: app sandbox boundaries, secure storage, authenticated network transport,
least privilege, log redaction, and dependency review. The OWASP Mobile
Application Security Verification Standard separates storage, network,
platform, code, resilience, and privacy controls [@owaspMasvs]; processing
locally addresses only part of that list. See @sec-security-authorization for
the broader trust and authorization model.

Fleet telemetry defaults to **content-free metrics**: deployment fingerprint,
route and reason, device tier, timing buckets, peak-memory bucket, thermal state,
load error, cancellation, and quality outcome when it can be collected without
content. Prompt or completion content is not collected by default. A debugging
program that needs examples must be separately authorized, narrowly sampled,
redacted, access-controlled, time-bounded, and removable. OpenTelemetry's
generative-AI conventions warn that model inputs and outputs are likely to
contain sensitive information [@otelGenAI].

## Deliver model versions safely

Large artifacts are often downloaded separately from the application. That
creates a software-update problem: incomplete downloads, corrupt storage,
rollback attacks, incompatible runtimes, low disk, and mixed versions of model,
tokenizer, and adapter. Treat the bundle as immutable and activate it only as a
complete set.

Each release needs a signed compatibility manifest containing artifact names,
sizes, cryptographic digest values, signature information, deployment
fingerprint, supported app and runtime versions, target device classes, and
expiry or retirement policy. The Update Framework formalizes signed metadata,
hash and size verification, version progression, and defenses against rollback,
freeze, and mix-and-match attacks; it is a useful model even when a platform's
asset service performs the transport [@tufSpec].

```{figure}
//| figure: bundle-slots
//| label: fig-edge-lifecycle
//| fig-cap: "One device takes a new bundle through two storage slots. The new version is downloaded into the inactive slot, verified against the signed manifest and smoke-tested there, and activated by one atomic pointer change; the last-known-good bundle stays in the other slot until the cohort is healthy, so a rollback is a second pointer change with nothing to download. The outcomes are a healthy rollout, a corrupt download rejected by its digest before activation, a cohort regression, and a device whose free space cannot hold a second bundle. Sizes, free space, and cohort metrics are illustrative."
```

Download beside the active bundle. Before activation, check free space and disk
quota, verify size, cryptographic digest, signature, compatibility manifest, and
license notices, then run a minimal load and golden-output smoke test. Use atomic
activation so a process sees either the old complete bundle or the new complete
bundle. Retain a last-known-good version until the rollout is healthy. Garbage
collection must not delete the active or rollback target, and it must cope with
an interrupted download.

Use a staged rollout by representative device tier, not only by account
percentage. Stop or roll back when load failures, crashes, quality rejection,
p95 latency, peak memory, energy, or thermal events cross their declared
thresholds. A server-side
kill switch can disable eligibility, but offline behavior must remain defined:
an installed unsafe version may require local disablement encoded in the app or
an expiry policy rather than a network response that never arrives.

## Operate the fleet

The procedure has eight steps:

1. **Freeze the envelope.** Record the task class, data boundary, quality
   threshold, supported device tiers, minimum OS, offline behavior, and fallback
   policy.
2. **Build the fingerprint.** Version the source checkpoint, tokenizer, prompt
   template, export graph, quantization configuration, compiled artifact,
   runtime, backend, and policy as one candidate.
3. **Qualify the complete artifact.** Check source-to-device parity, task quality,
   operator coverage, CPU fallback, storage, peak resident memory, and every
   acceptance-matrix cell.
4. **Benchmark sustained behavior.** Measure cold and warm latency, p50 and p95,
   energy per accepted task, memory pressure, and thermal steady state on
   representative device tiers.
5. **Inject device failures.** Exercise model unavailable, offline start, weak
   network, low storage, corrupt download, backend rejection, cancellation,
   background load, and thermal throttling.
6. **Stage delivery.** Verify the inactive bundle, activate atomically for a
   small device-tier cohort, and compare against the last-known-good release.
7. **Observe and roll back.** Monitor content-free route, quality, reliability,
   latency, energy, and thermal signals; roll back on the recorded thresholds.
8. **Register each requalification trigger.** Repeat the affected matrix when
   the model, tokenizer, template, quantization, exporter, runtime, backend,
   operating system, device policy, or support envelope changes.

NIST's generative-AI profile treats deployment-context evaluation,
post-deployment monitoring, incident response, change management, and
decommissioning as lifecycle work rather than one-time release checks
[@nist2024gairmf], and the procedure above applies that view to device
deployments. @sec-eval-practice provides the quality and observability method,
while @sec-deployment-lifecycle develops staged release and rollback in more
detail.

The output is a deployment decision record: the envelope, exact fingerprint,
acceptance matrix, measured results, privacy data flow, routing policy, delivery
plan, rollback thresholds, owner, and requalification triggers. It supports a
local release, a hybrid release, or a documented decision not to ship on-device.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

Three boundaries remain empirical. First, local versus cloud is a feature-level
choice: device capability can improve while remote models and networks improve
too. Second, accelerator portability remains limited by operator coverage,
compiler behavior, and vendor runtimes; a common source model does not imply one
common executable. Third, very-low-bit training can change the quality-memory
frontier, but published model-level gains do not guarantee system-level latency
or energy gains on a target device. The acceptance matrix records these as
alternatives to measure, instead of building forecasts about them into the
architecture.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

The device budget reaches backward through the entire stack. Memory and thermal
limits influence model architecture and context length. Kernel availability
influences quantization. Export and operator coverage influence training-time
choices. Privacy and offline policy influence routing and telemetry. Two-bit
quantization-aware training writes the memory budget into the training
objective, and training a small model far past the compute-optimal token count
writes the lifetime inference cost into the training budget. The device
therefore constrains where inference runs and also which model can be trained,
represented, delivered, observed, and safely updated.
:::
